newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia govt plans to recoup A$1 bln budget loss.
newsitem.headline: Australia govt plans to recoup A$1 bln budget loss.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello said in a newspaper interview on Saturday that he planned to use next May's budget to recover about A$1 billion lost when the Senate rejected some of this year's budget.

In an interview with The Weekend Australian, Costello also said 1997 would be the year of micro-economic reform, with the government introducing changes in the finance, transport, energy and labour market areas.

Costello described the 1996 budget as the "major fiscal consolidation of our time" but said the Senate's defeat of some individual budget measures meant the government had lost about A$1 billion in fiscal tightening in its second and third years.
This August's budget was designed to make budget savings of around A$36 billion over four years.
"We'll have to address that loss of savings," Costello told the newspaper.
"But we won't be announcing how we'll respond to that until we've considered the mid-year review and we'll announce how we respond to that in the course of next year's budget."

He added: "This is the major fiscal consolidation of our time. We've taken on a A$10 billion (annual) deficit, we've put Australia back on track to a surplus over the lifetime of this government...(and) we've managed to take the public with us and to increase our support.
"This has defied every political nostrum that the way to get public support is to spend more."

Although Australia's conservative coalition has a solid majority in the lower house of parliament, it has depended on the support of two independent MPs to pass legislation through the Senate and has seen some budget bills amended.

The newspaper said its interview was conducted on Wednesday, before an attack on the pace of the government's economic reforms by Australian-born media magnate Rupert Murdoch, who said the country risked becoming an economic backwater.
Costello said A$400 million worth of measures to crack down on welfare payments to migrants would be put back to the Senate and, if rejected, would be reintroduced three months later.
Such a move could provide a trigger for a double dissolution of Australia's two houses of parliament and a fresh election, the newspaper said.
It added that Costello said the government would also seek new negotiations on A$400 million in social security measures over four years.
